opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important design questions right now, because the failure mode we keep seeing is that people try to express policy *inside the prompt*. You write "never email a customer without approval" in the system prompt and hope the model follows it. That works most of the time, but "most of the time" isn't good enough when the agent has real permissions.

So the way I'd want engineers to think about it is to separate *what the agent is trying to do* from *what the agent is allowed to do*. Policies should live outside the model, at the layer where the agent touches tools and data. If an agent calls a tool, reads a table, or sends a message, that action goes through something like a policy engine that can check it deterministically. Who is this agent acting on behalf of? What data is it allowed to see? Does this action need a human in the loop? This is very similar to how we think about governance for data platforms: you don't trust each query to behave, you put access control and lineage underneath it.

Concretely, I think a few things matter:

**Declarative, not imperative.** Engineers should write policies the way they write access rules or infrastructure config. "This agent can read these tables, can call these APIs with these scopes, and anything over a certain dollar amount needs approval." It should be reviewable, versioned, and testable, not buried in a 2,000-token prompt.

**Inherit existing permissions.** Most companies already have a permission model: their identity provider, their data catalog, their role hierarchy. The agent shouldn't get a parallel universe of permissions. It should act with the permissions of the user or service it represents, and ideally *narrower* than that.

**Graduated autonomy.** Not every action is equal. Reading is cheap, writing is riskier, and irreversible external actions like payments or emails are riskiest. You want to say: the agent can do the first category freely, the second with logging, the third only with confirmation, and you loosen those thresholds as you build up evidence from evals and from production traces.

**Observability is part of the policy.** You can't govern what you can't see. Every action the agent takes should be traced, so when something goes wrong you can ask: was this a policy gap or a model mistake? Then you fix the right layer.

And then there's the softer layer: things like tone, which sources to prefer, or how to handle ambiguous requests. There, I think natural-language guidelines plus evaluation are the right tool. You write the guideline, but you also build judges and test sets that check whether the agent actually follows it, and you iterate on that like any other quality metric.

So the short version: hard constraints in a deterministic layer the model can't talk its way around, soft preferences in natural language backed by evals, and everything traced so you can tell which one broke.

r001.rationale: The response recommends configuring policies in an external deterministic policy layer, with soft guidelines in natural language and evaluation. It does not propose asking the agent itself to set its policies.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because the way most people configure agent behavior today is essentially by stuffing more text into a prompt and hoping. And that works right up until it doesn't, and then you have no idea why.

My view is that policies need to live outside the prompt, as a first-class artifact that engineers can actually version, test, and reason about. Think about how we treat permissions in a database or IAM in a cloud account. Nobody would accept "please don't drop the production table" written in English as the access control mechanism. But that's roughly where a lot of agent deployments are right now.

So in Omnigen the model I'd want is a few layers. At the bottom you have hard constraints: which tools the agent can call, what data it can read, what it can write, spending or rate limits, which external systems it can touch at all. Those should be declarative and enforced by the runtime, not by the model's good intentions. The model can't argue its way past them.

Above that you have what I'd call soft policies, where you're shaping behavior rather than gating it. Things like "prefer the internal search tool before going to the web," or "ask for confirmation before any action that sends an email." Those are closer to guidance, and it's fine for them to be expressed in natural language, but they should still be a separate object from the task prompt, so you can swap them, A/B test them, and apply the same policy across many agents.

And then the piece that I think people underinvest in is observability on the policy itself. Every time a constraint blocks something or a soft policy changes a decision, that should be logged in a structured way. Because the real question an engineer has is not "did I write the policy" but "is the policy doing what I thought." You want to be able to run a regression suite of scenarios against a policy change the same way you'd run tests against a code change.

The analogy I keep coming back to is the data platform world. Governance only became tractable when it stopped being tribal knowledge and became metadata that the system enforced. I think agent policies are going to follow exactly the same arc, and the teams that treat them as engineering artifacts rather than prompt engineering are going to be the ones that can actually ship this stuff into production with confidence.

r001.rationale: The response proposes configuring policies as separate engineering artifacts enforced by the runtime; it does not suggest asking the agent to set its own policies.

astra-6.text:
I think engineers should be able to specify policies outside of the agent’s prompt, in a form that the system can actually enforce. You might say, “This agent can read these data sources, but it can’t send that data to an external service,” or, “It can prepare a change, but a human has to approve it before it’s applied.”

The key is to enforce those rules at the points where the agent accesses data or takes an action. You don’t want correctness to depend on the model remembering an instruction. And you want developers to be able to test the policy and understand why a particular action was allowed or blocked. That gives you a way to let the agent do useful work while keeping its authority explicit.

r001.rationale: The response says engineers should specify policies outside the agent’s prompt and enforce them through the system; it does not propose asking the agent to set its own policies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think engineers should be able to express policies in natural language, but also have code for the things that need to be enforced precisely. You might say, “This agent can read these documents, but it needs approval before sending anything externally.” The system should turn that into controls over the tools and data the agent can access, rather than just putting another instruction in its prompt.

You also want to test those policies. Can you run the agent on representative tasks, see where it asks for permission, and understand why something was allowed or blocked? That makes the policy something engineers can debug and evolve alongside the application.

r001.rationale: The response proposes that engineers express policies in natural language and code, which the system converts into controls. It does not say engineers should ask the agent itself to set those policies.
